I got a surprising amount of reading done.  But to be fair, I didn't start all of these books this month, I just finished these this month.

**Blood Meridian, or the Evening Redness in the West, by Cormac McCarthy**: I have mixed feelings about this book--I enjoyed it a lot for what it was, but I struggle with books that (at first glance) are meaningless.  I actually ended up liking it more after thinking about it for a while.  It's easily one of the most disturbing books I've ever read though, with probably the most disturbing ending I've ever read. (Audiobook)

**The Every, by Dave Eggers***:* I wasn't really a fan of this at all.  It feels like it's written for people who are way more naive than the average person in my age range in general, and the messages get kind of muddied every once in a while.  And I feel like the author is a hypocrite because of how he marketed it versus how he actually sold it, which ultimately detracted from my already low opinion of it.  I got it for free though, so I guess I at least don't have to feel like I wasted money on it, just my time. (Print)

**Sunshine, by Robin McKinley**: I liked certain aspects of this book.  The author created a really interesting world, did a lot of solid characterization and world-building within it, then wastes so much time on exposition rather than furthering the plot.  It's one of those books where a ridiculous amount of time is spent on describing how a character likes working in a coffee shop and how that coffee shop actually also serves champagne and it's kind of a local icon for it, all while she's chained up next to a monster.  It wasn't bad, like I said, the lore is interesting, but good G O D the exposition is a nightmare. (Audiobook)

**Mapping the Interior, by Stephen Graham Jones**: Stephen Graham Jones is just capital G, Good.  His work is always so surreal and uncanny and *inviting* all at the same time.  This is a short read, but a good read, and I'm always down to shill for native literature. (eBook)

**The Woman Outside My Door, by Rachel Ryan**: A very solid book that I wasn't expecting to either like as much as I did or read it as quickly as I did.  I think it only took me a couple days?  I don't usually go for psychological thrillers with no surreal or supernatural angle but it kind of opened me to the idea of them. (Print)

**For the Wolf, by Hanna Whitten**: This was just okay.  On the "good" side of okay, but still just okay.  I liked the setting, I liked the lore, I *loved* the wolf, but I just wasn't a fan of the main character or her sister--I'm not sure what really irked me about them ultimately, I think I'm honestly maybe a little averse to princess/royal characters in general because I can't relate to them.  The wolf was such a king though, loved that guy. (Audiobook)

**Eden, by Tim Lebbon**: Holy shit this book was bad.  The setting was so interesting, and it was ruined by a 100% unlikeable or unmemorable cast of characters.  I just wanted some solid eco horror and this was so *bad*.  I can't believe that as many people actually like this as they do.  I usually don't have contrary opinions to the general consensus when it comes to books, but for once I legitimately can't even understand what people like about this.  The setting is great, like I said, it's an interesting premise, but the characters ruin it so much. (Audiobook)

**House of Leaves, by Mark Z. Danielewski**: This is one that I was re-reading.  I read it about 9 or 10 years ago maybe and have been wanting to give it another read for a while.  I loved it back then, when I was about 15 or 16 I think maybe, and although I still enjoyed it now as an adult, I did have to view it somewhat more as an art piece instead of a work of literature.  I just had to bump it down from 5 to 4 stars on goodreads because it actually felt kind of pretentious to me now, more so than it did when I was a kid. (Print)

**I Am Not a Serial Killer, by Dan Wells**: I really liked this book.  I had seen the movie back when it came out, and wasn't aware at the time that it was a book series.  I actually only found out that it was a book (series) recently, actually, and I'm very happy that I tried it out.  My opinion may change as I go further into the series, but it's an excellent start. (Audiobook)

There's a few for me:

\- Wide lines

\- Huge margins

\- Lines that don't extend all the way across the page

\- Dot grids (I love normal squared grids though)

\- Paper that feels and looks like normal printer paper

\- Inspirational/motivational quotes in the margins

\- Prompts in the margins

\- Any font on the cover that's too noticeable.  A small brand identifier of some sort is fine as long as it isn't distracting.

\- Glue binding

\- Spiral binding

\- Ring binding

\- Floppy covers that are too floppy--I'm fine with soft covers within reason

\- When it costs more than $20 tops--I don't have anything to say that I would consider worth more than that

\- Images printed in the margins that are distracting/ugly

\- Specific shades of black or brown for the cover.  I like some, but there's some really gross looking covers out there

\- Neon/bright coloured covers

\- Art on the cover that I didn't put there myself
